title: Poor or rich (Avot 4:9)
hookLine: a gym habit that only lasts while life is easy: Yonatan says keep Torah in poverty and you'll keep it in wealth
tomorrow: too busy to breathe. what does Rabbi Meir say to cut?

cards: Does the practice go when the money goes? It's often the first thing to go: the class, the lessons, the long run, the habit that only lived while life was easy. Then the budget comes back, and the habit doesn't.
Rabbi Yonatan has a line about exactly that, and on first hearing it seems backwards. Keep it when you're poor, he says, and you'll keep it when you're rich. Why would hard times come first?

teach.h: KEEP IT POOR, KEEP IT RICH.
teach.b: Here's the whole saying, in plain words. Whoever keeps the Torah in poverty will in the end keep it in wealth. And whoever neglects the Torah in wealth will in the end neglect it in poverty.
Now the odd detail. You'd expect a promise about money: be faithful when broke and you'll get rich. Some readers do hear it that way.
But look at what actually carries across the line. Not the money. The keeping.
Each half is a forecast about a habit. What you do with the Torah on a thin week is what you'll do with it on a full one. And the second half closes the escape hatch.

Plenty is not a better time to start. Whoever lets it slide when they have everything will let it slide when they have nothing, too. Some readers take poverty and wealth more widely than a bank balance.

teach.h: NEGLECT IT RICH, NEGLECT IT POOR.
teach.b: Poor in time, rich in time. Poor in energy, rich in spare hours.

teach.h: IT'S A FORECAST ABOUT A HABIT.
teach.b: Either way, the puzzle solves itself the same way: hard times come first because that's where the habit is actually built.
A practice that only survives easy weeks was never really yours. One that survived a hard week will still be there when things open up.
Poor or rich, it's the same practice.

how: Many Jews keep a fixed time for study, even a few minutes a day, and the custom is to keep it in busy or lean seasons as well as easy ones.

o: keep a practice in hard times and you'll keep it in good ones
give your money away and God will make you wealthy
the poor and the rich keep different laws of the Torah

games.q: the two halves — tap the pairs.

s: the saying promises you'll get rich if you keep the Torah
some hear it that way, but what carries across the line is the keeping, not the money.
a good season is the safest time to start a practice
the second half says whoever lets it slide in plenty will let it slide in want, too.
some readers take poverty and wealth to include time and energy
poor in time or rich in spare hours: the forecast about the habit works the same.

games.q: exam month: you're sleeping five hours and your nightly ten minutes of reading is the first thing on the chopping block. what does Rabbi Yonatan's line suggest?
o: keep a one-minute version every night, so the habit survives the hard month.
pause it completely and restart in summer, when you'll have time to do it right.
double it now, since hardship earns a bigger reward later on.
games.why: the saying is a forecast about habits: what you keep on a thin week is what you'll keep on a full one. a small version still counts as keeping.

practice: Choose one practice you keep, or mean to keep: a few minutes of study, a blessing before you eat, this lesson. Name the hard week that would most likely knock it out.
Then make a plan for the smallest version that could survive that week, one minute, one line, one breath, and say it to yourself once: when that week comes, I'll do the small version.

wordCard.voice: Poor or rich. Rabbi Yonatan's saying: keep the Torah in a hard time and you'll keep it in a good one.

orig.note: Hebrew: from poverty, from wealth, the two poles of Rabbi Yonatan's saying.

carryVoice: For the road: poor or rich, the same practice, built on the thin weeks. That's day thirty-one of sixty.

sources.ref: Mishnah Avot 4:9 (Rabbi Yonatan: whoever keeps the Torah in poverty will keep it in wealth)
